transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-10-21
Start: 16:00 PT | Duration: 52 mins
Attendees: Alex Romero, Samira Khan, Ethan Li (Redwood); Dr. Priya Patel, Jordan Mills, Tara Nguyen, Marcus Reed (Cascade)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
- Focus: scorecard calibration + bias audits
- Action: additional labels, run dedicated regression, share rubric + security details

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Okay, thanks everyone for joining. I think we've got 50 minutes, we'll try to run through the updated scorecard and then jump into the bias slices after. Priya, you had flagged a couple of high level concerns in the slack thread, is that still top of mind?
[00:12] Dr. Patel (Cascade): Yeah thanks Alex, the main thing for us is we saw a drift in the scorecard for clinical triage responses last week — more false positives where the model suggested escalation where clinicians didn't think it was needed. We want to understand whether that's prompt changes, the model variant, or an evaluation quirk.
[00:28] Samira (Redwood SE): Right, we pulled the batch from your test set and did a quick bisect. There's a cluster tied to longer prompt context plus an older few-shot format. The KV cache — sorry, kay vee cache interactions — seemed to surface repeated context that nudged the model toward escalation language.
[00:46] Jordan (Cascade, Data Eng): Interesting, we didn't expect the context carryover to be that big. We do client-side concatenation of notes so sequence length is pretty variable.
[00:58] Ethan (Redwood): Quick note — we tested both hosted and dedicated variants. Latency was fine on hosted but cost per token creeped up on long contexts; Dedicated showed more stable per-token cost and allowed us to pin quantization profile without an accuracy hit.
[01:12] Tara (Cascade, Clinical QA): Is there any chance the few-shot examples are biasing the system? Some of the examples are skewed toward more conservative escalation.
[01:22] Samira: That was my hunch. The few-shot exemplars in your prompt set lean toward escalation decisions; when you combine that with repeated context it amplifies the escalation signature. We recommended pruning the few-shot set to a balanced slice.
[01:36] Marcus (Cascade, Security): Before we get too far, we need to confirm audit logging format. For compliance the SOC-2 folks require a machine-readable export of prompts, model id, and response hashes for 90 days. Is that something Redwood can provide from Hosted or only Dedicated/Private?
[01:53] Alex: Good question. Hosted can provide request-level logs for 30 days by default; Dedicated/Private gives you the retention controls and raw audit export. We'll send the exact schema; Samira I'll ping you to include the current field names (model_name, model_version, request_id, timestamp, prompt_hash, response_hash).
[02:12] Jordan: Also, on the scoring side, our rubric had a single "escalation_correctness" score but we think we need finer granularity: clinical urgency vs. suggested action vs. conservative phrasing.
[02:25] Alex: We updated the scorecard to split those slices — urgency, actionability, and phrasing. You'll see weights. Let me walk through the CSV quick.
[02:33] [screen share noise] Alex: (reading) Row one is example_id, ground_truth_action, model_action, urgency_score (0-1), actionability_score (0-1), phrasing_penalty, overall. The overall is a weighted sum, default weights are 0.5 urgency, 0.3 actionability, 0.2 phrasing.
[03:00] Dr. Patel: That seems reasonable but I want to raise bias concerns. For certain patient cohorts (age and comorbidity) we saw higher escalation rates. Can we add fairness slices to the scorecard?
[03:13] Samira: Yes, we added demographic slices — age_bucket, chronic_condition_flag, language_preference. The scorecard can break out metrics per slice and produce delta from baseline.
[03:24] Tara: When you say language_preference, is that detected from notes or from a field? We worry about false flags if detection is noisy.
[03:32] Samira: For now it's a field from your dataset, not auto-detected. If you want, we can run a small detection job but that'll add noise. Better to use curated labels for fairness tests.
[03:42] Jordan: We'll provide labels. We're planning to pull an additional 200 examples across underrepresented cohorts and label them. That should help.
[03:49] Marcus: Back to security — is prompt contents stored in cleartext in hosted logs? We need to know encryption at rest and KMS integration.
[03:59] Alex: Hosted stores logs encrypted at rest and in transit; we rotate keys, but for customer-managed KMS we'd recommend Dedicated/Private. We'll attach our SOC-2 and KMS integration docs.
[04:12] [05:20] Samira (Redwood SE): I want to flag one concrete regression case — example id cascade-3312. The model hallucinates a prior admission that isn't in the notes and suggests escalation. The pattern was introduced after a prompt formatting tweak where an extra delimiter was added. I'll drop a reproducible snippet into the shared folder after this call.
[05:35] Dr. Patel: That was one that worried us. If it's prompt-format related, can we recommend a canonical serializer? We've seen newline vs pipe delimiters change the model behavior.
[05:46] Ethan: On our side we generally recommend JSONL context with explicit keys (e.g., "note_text": "...", "timestamp": "...") so the model sees structured markers; that reduces hallucination from concatenated free text. But I know in practice teams use different inline formats.
[06:02] Jordan: We'll evaluate switching to JSONL for a subset. For now we'll annotate examples with the current concatenated format so the regression run reflects real traffic.
[06:12] Tara: For the fairness slices, what's the sample size minimum for stable stats? 200 enough?
[06:20] Samira: 200 per slice is a bare minimum to get signal; 500 is better. Given time constraints 200 should show major gaps. We'll mark the confidence intervals in the dashboard.
[06:32] Alex: Okay so action items recap: Redwood sends updated scorecard, SE shares repro for cascade-3312, Cascade provides 200 labeled examples, Security will confirm retention. Anything else?
[06:43] Marcus: Also need to confirm export format — CSV or Parquet? Our audit tooling prefers Parquet with typed columns.
[06:51] Alex: We can provide both; we'll include Parquet export in the Dedicated docs.
[07:00] Dr. Patel: One other ask — can you run the proposed regression on a Dedicated replica with the same quantization profile? We want to see unit cost and quality tradeoff with the pinned profile.
[07:10] Samira: Yes we'll spin a dedicated test instance (test-3) using the same q4_0 profile you tested earlier, then run the labeled set and return the scorecard. Expect initial results in 5 business days.
[07:22] Jordan: On metrics, can we get token-level latency and per-example per-component timing (prompt serialization time, model infer time)? That helps us isolate pipeline vs model issues.
[07:33] Ethan: Yes the Console exposes per-route breakdowns; we'll include a sample tracing CSV.
[07:40] [08:05] Alex: Quick note on competing approaches — we saw Anthropic doing a safety-tuned few-shot pattern; Vertex has auto-scaling with cheaper preemptibles but less control. Noted for context, not a recommendation.
[08:17] Tara: For guardrails, we want to add a hard-check: if model suggests escalation and confidence < 0.6, default to clinician review. Can Redwood enforce soft/hard fallback rules?
[08:28] Samira: Yes, we have routing policies—soft fallbacks can add a warning; hard fallbacks can route to a human queue or block automated escalation. That routing policy is configurable per route in the Console.
[08:41] Marcus: And will those fallbacks be logged for audit?
[08:44] Alex: Logged, yes — fallback reason, model confidence, and route decision will be in the audit export.
[08:50] Dr. Patel: Great. I also want to flag a potential bias where older patients are escalated more often, could be correlation with comorbidity. We'll need intersectional slices.
[09:02] Samira: We'll add an intersectional check (age_bucket x chronic_condition_flag) to the scorecard delta.
[09:09] Jordan: On the practical side, when do you need the labels? We can start labeling semi-manually this week.
[09:16] Alex: Ideally by Monday of next week so Redwood can run the regression on Tuesday. So target 2025-10-27 as Jordan noted earlier.
[09:24] [10:00] Samira: I'll paste an example PR for the few-shot pruning rules — basically remove duplicates, balance classes, and clamp exemplar language to neutral phrasing.
[10:11] Tara: That makes sense. For the neutral phrasing clamp, do you have an automatic sanitizer or is it manual?
[10:17] Samira: We can provide a lightweight sanitizer script that normalizes phrasing, but we'd want human review on clinical statements. We'll share the script; it's not a full clinical rewrite.
[10:27] Alex: OK let's recap formal next steps: 1) Redwood send scorecard + rubric (CSV), 2) Samira share repro and sanitizer script, 3) Cascade to deliver 200 labeled examples, 4) Redwood run Dedicated regression test and return results.
[10:44] Dr. Patel: Sounds good. One last tiny item — can Redwood document the exact model variant name used in the runs (e.g., "redwood-3-1b-q4_0") so we can pin it in our reproducibility notes?
[10:55] Ethan: Yes all runs embed model_name and model_version in the export; we'll make sure the run artifact includes that.
[11:05] Alex: Perfect. We'll follow up via email and I'll drop the scorecard in the shared Drive. Thanks everyone, see you next week.
[11:12] [end]
